What is a menstrual cup?

A menstrual cup is typically a medical grade silicon cup that is inserted into the vagina to collect menstrual blood. They have been around in some form since the 1920s (iirc) and while you have been doling out hundreds over the years on pads and tampons, NGOs have been giving these out to illegals and "refugee" women. I bought my first menstrual cup for $35 after tracing down one of these companies donating to the NGOs. For me, it was not only significant money savings, but more comfortable, almost no odor, more hygienic and a welcome reduction in waste.

Is a menstrual cup right for me?

A menstrual cup is not porous and does not harbor disease. As long as your vagina's microfauna is in balance, using a cup should cause you no aggravation in the way of yeast infections, vaginosis, etc.

As far as pain and cramping, the cup buttresses the vaginal wall so you may find the vagina can't spasm as hard.

There are a million ways to insert the cup wrong and cause discomfort. The cup may also cause discomfort if it is interacting with a mass like a fibroid.

Menstrual cups also come in a variety of shapes and sizes so you can probably find one that fits you best.

How does the cup stay in?

Your kegals will pull the cup into place and suction will keep it there. When it fills up enough, it will get heavy and start to slide down and leak a bit and you know the cup is full and needs to be emptied.

You should be aware that the cup may leak a bit and wear a panty liner. The cup can also lose its suction from a sneeze or strange motion and need to be reinserted.

How to insert the cup?

*This is the hard part. There is a learning curve. If you are new to using cups, I recommend practicing towards the end of your cycle when your flow is lighter. *

You need to fold your cup to make it small enough to fit into the vaginal opening. The rigidity and ease of folding varies with brands. Once you get it folded securely, you have to find an angle of insertion that works for you. You will probably make a mess and put it in crooked the first time. It may help to hold the labia open with the other hand. As you get the hang of it, you will be able to insert the cup with out getting your hands dirty.

Next, you need to make the cup form a suction. You can rotate the cup or lightly plunge the vagina a few times to make the cup expand fully. Then push the cup further in the vaginal canal and you should hear and feel the air escaping out of the cup. Give the cup a little tug to feel if it sealed. Once you get the hang of it, it will just take seconds to get it in.

To empty...

Push the cup out, pinch the bottom to completely pull it out and break the suction and dump into the toilet. Wipe the outside of the cup and reinsert.

How to clean your cup

Soap and warm water is all you need. It will tolerate a boil if you have a mishap and it falls in the toilet. To deodorize and remove strains, soak the cup in a bit of peroxide. To store the cup, you can use a lint free satchel but I prefer a glass jar.
